newsitem.title: SRI LANKA: Sri Lanka watchdog takes media bill to court.
newsitem.headline: Sri Lanka watchdog takes media bill to court.

text.p: A Sri Lankan media watchdog on Wednesday petitioned the Supreme Court over proposed broadcast legislation seen by opponents as an effort to stifle freedom of speech.

The bill, introduced in parliament last week, seeks to set up a broadcasting authority with wide powers to monitor, regulate and grant operating licences to radio and television broadcasters. The Supreme Court must rule in three weeks.

"We're challenging the bill on the grounds that it contravenes constitutional provisions with regard to the right of free expression, that it imposes unnecessary restrictions on the right of free expression," Lucien Rajakarunanayake, a trustee of the Free Media Movement (FMM), told Reuters.
The proposed authority will pave the way for complete control by the government over the electronic media, Rajakarunanayake said.

"This is quite contrary to the recommendations made by the special committee appointed by the media minister to recommend changes to all laws governing the media to bring about a more democratic media culture in Sri Lanka," he added.
The main opposition United National Party (UNP), media groups and some members of the ruling People's Alliance (PA) have lambasted the bill.

The UNP on Tuesday petitioned the Supreme Court, saying the bill was unconstitutional. Officials at two private television stations said their organisations had either petitioned the court or planned to do so.
UNP sources said the bill was doomed if the Supreme Court ruled it needed a two-thirds vote in parliament, because the ruling PA, with a one-seat majority, would find it hard to pass the bill.
The UNP last week objected to the inclusion of the defence secretary in the proposed authority's board of directors, saying the military's growing role was a cause of concern.

Sri Lanka's government, fighting Tamil rebels demanding independence for minority Tamils in the north and east of the island, has warned private radio and television stations against broadcasting news that could create ethnic disharmony.
Sri Lanka has eight television stations -- two owned by the government -- and about a dozen radio stations, most of them privately owned.
